name: Rosa Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, happy to. I talk about this stuff constantly anyway, my partner Dev is sick of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle unemployment benefit claims at the benefits office in town, the one above the post office. Last year I put my hand up for the pilot team testing a triage tool, which sorts new claims by how urgent and how complicated they are. So half my day is normal casework, interviews, checking work histories, and half is flagging where the tool got it wrong. I use an AI assistant every day for drafting notes and working out tricky rules. What I love is when someone walks out with money coming that week. What drains me is how slow everything is to change, even when everyone agrees it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I've seen what these tools can do on the pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown but the small wins are real. On the pilot we cut the time to sort a new claim from twenty minutes to about five. I'd post that online, because people swing between thinking it's magic and thinking it's useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. My job's safe, my skills are a bit ahead of the office, and Dev's teaching job isn't going anywhere. The one thing is that I'd probably get bored, and I'd start wondering if public service is moving too slowly for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to roll the triage tool out to the whole office, since it'd be one of the few useful bits. I'd keep saving about two hundred a month and maybe do a short evening course in data, just because I like it. Otherwise, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of restlessness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get bored. What would that lead to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably looking at jobs on the digital services team at the ministry, building the tools instead of testing them. It's a move I'd make anyway at some point. A plateau would just give me less reason to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that would still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. Our landlord put it up twice in two years. But we've got about five months saved and two steady jobs, so it's a grumble rather than a worry.

say: I'd say the hype was **overblown** but the small wins are real.
I'd post that the pilot cut claim sorting from **twenty minutes to five**.
think: My job is safe and my **skills** are a bit ahead of the office.
My real risk is **boredom** and feeling public service moves too slowly for me.
do: Push to roll the **triage tool** out to the whole office.
Keep saving about **two hundred a month** toward our cushion.
Take a short **evening course** in data for interest.
S0.quote: On the pilot we cut the time to sort a new claim from twenty minutes to about five.
fieldNote: She's the rare caseworker who'd be **disappointed** by a plateau.
Two steady incomes and about **five months saved** make her genuinely secure here.
Her pull toward **building tools** shows up even when nothing pushes her.

steps.text: Push to roll the claim triage tool out office-wide
Keep saving about two hundred a month
Take a short evening course in data analysis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is basically what the pilot feels like if you scale it up. I can see it happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools are good but the jobs need protecting, and those two things aren't in conflict. I'd push for the union to have a seat on how they're rolled out. Online I'd argue for public ownership of the software, so a private firm doesn't own how benefits get decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the people who comes out alright. I know the tools, I know where they fail, and that knowledge is suddenly worth something. But I'd feel guilty, because the people who can't or won't learn them are my friends on the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the digital services team at the ministry within the year, the ones who design the claim system. Before that I'd do the data course properly, the six-month one, about eight hundred in fees. And I'd run lunch sessions for the team on how to check the tool's work, so fewer people get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at the same time. Like being on a fast train that might not stop at everyone's station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman on my team, twenty-two years in, who prints every email. She's brilliant with claimants and terrified of the screen. If the job becomes supervising software, she's the one they'll quietly push out, and she's better at the human bit than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever say no to a promotion that came from replacing people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, honestly, but I'd use it to argue for keeping the people who are good with claimants. I'm not naive. Someone is going to design these systems, and I'd rather it's someone who's sat across from a person who just lost their job.

say: I'd say good tools and **protected jobs** aren't in conflict.
Online I'd argue for **public ownership** of the software that decides benefits.
think: I expect to come out alright because I know **where the tools fail**.
I'd feel **guilty** about colleagues who can't or won't learn them.
do: Apply to the ministry's **digital services team** within the year.
Finish a **six-month data course**, about eight hundred in fees.
Run **lunch sessions** teaching colleagues to check the tool's work.
feel: **Excited** and uneasy at once, like a fast train that may skip stations.
S1.quote: Someone is going to design these systems, and I'd rather it's someone who's sat across from a person who just lost their job.
fieldNote: She expects to **benefit personally**, and that comes with real guilt about colleagues.
Her progressive outlook shows as **public ownership** of software, not opposition to it.
She'd teach colleagues to **check the tool**, trying to soften the cut from inside.

steps.text: Apply to the ministry's digital services team within a year
Complete the six-month data course for about eight hundred
Run lunch sessions teaching colleagues to check the triage tool
Push the union for a seat on how tools are rolled out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one is different. Two years is not enough for anyone, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need emergency laws now: a public income floor, a pause on cutting front-line benefits jobs, and public control of the systems. I'd write to my representative and I'd go to the protests. People who need benefits will need them more than ever, and the offices shouldn't vanish at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my head start doesn't help much here. If AI can do almost any thinking work, it can do the designing and checking I was planning to move into. I'd have maybe a year longer than the people on my team, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still move to the digital services team straight away, because a year is a year. I'd put every bonus and spare bit of pay into savings to stretch our five months to eight. And I'd start looking at work that's mostly people, like running a community advice project, since robots that can do hands-on and face-to-face work come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but sort of focused. I'd be making lists at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a year longer than your team. Is that a comfort or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It means I'd watch my colleagues go first and then follow them. That's not a nice year to look forward to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's job is teaching, which is part thinking work and part managing thirty teenagers in a room. We'd probably lean on his salary and stop talking about a deposit. We'd also stop talking about a dog, which sounds silly, but it would be the first thing I'd notice.

say: I'd demand **emergency laws**: an income floor and a pause on cutting front-line jobs.
I'd **write to my representative** and join protests for public control of the systems.
think: My **head start** barely helps, because AGI can do the design work too.
I'd get maybe **a year longer** than my team, not a career.
do: Move to the **digital services team** straight away for the extra year.
Save every spare bit of pay to stretch savings from **five to eight months**.
Look for **people-focused work**, like running a community advice project.
feel: **Anxious but focused**, making lists at midnight.
S2.quote: If AI can do almost any thinking work, it can do the designing and checking I was planning to move into.
fieldNote: Even her **adaptability** runs out against a two-year AGI, and she says so plainly.
She'd lean on her partner's **teaching salary**, which is part hands-on and buys time.
She keeps acting even when **pessimistic**, which sets her apart from her calmer pictures.

steps.text: Move to the ministry's digital services team straight away
Put spare pay into savings to stretch the cushion to eight months
Write to her representative and join protests for an income floor
Look into running a community advice project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That changes my plan a lot compared with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well, if we start now. I'd push the union to get a deal on retraining for every caseworker, not just the keen ones. And I'd say loudly that the systems should be public, with a person anyone can appeal to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get somewhere useful, but I'm not sure where useful is. The design jobs go by 2031 too. The thing I keep landing on is that what's left is the bit where people are in a room together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two years on the digital services team, learning how government buys and runs these systems, then move into community work around 2029. I'd do a part-time course in community development alongside. And I'd keep saving, maybe enough for a year without pay by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a manageable way. It's a hard question but not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Community work pays less than casework. How would you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd live smaller. No car, a cheaper flat, maybe further out of town. I'd rather earn less doing something people need than more doing something a machine will do next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the woman on your team who prints every email?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to take whatever retraining is offered in year one, not year four, and I'd sit with her through it. Honestly, she'd be great at community work, better than me. I'd try to take her with me.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **do this well** if we start now.
I'd push for **retraining for every caseworker** and public systems with a person to appeal to.
think: Five years helps, but the **design jobs** go by 2031 too.
What's left is the work where **people** are **in a room** together.
do: Spend **two years** on the digital services team, then move on around 2029.
Take a **part-time course** in community development alongside.
Save enough for **a year without pay** by 2030.
feel: **Anxious** in a manageable way, a hard question rather than an emergency.
S3.quote: I'd rather earn less doing something people need than more doing something a machine will do next year.
fieldNote: She treats the digital team as a **stepping stone**, not the destination.
Her answer to AGI is **people work**, accepting lower pay and a smaller life.
She'd try to bring an **older colleague** with her, a thread through all her answers.

steps.text: Work two years on the digital services team to learn the systems
Take a part-time community development course
Save enough to cover a year without pay by 2030
Push the union for retraining for every caseworker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career chapter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best case, and it's still a huge change. I'd campaign for the boring, solid stuff: a retraining right for every worker, a public option for these tools, and benefit offices with real people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of the first five or six years, and I'd use them to build something that lasts. The question is whether I have the discipline to leave a good job before I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend three or four years on the digital services team, then use what I've learned to set up a community advice service with a couple of others, maybe as a co-op. I'd save hard while I'm on the better salary. And I'd keep using every new tool, because knowing them is my edge for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a small cold spot about the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said for now. When does that end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around 2034, when even the people who run the systems are being run by them. That's when I want to already be in the community work. Understanding the tools is my edge until it isn't. Being early is my one real skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any big life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably buy somewhere around 2029, while I'm on the better salary. Dev and I have talked about kids, and with ten years I'd feel okay doing that too, maybe 2030.

say: I'd say ten years is the **best case** and still a huge change.
I'd campaign for a **retraining right**, a public option for tools, and staffed benefit offices.
think: I'd **do well** in the first five or six years and build something lasting.
The question is whether I'll **leave a good job** before I have to.
do: Spend **three or four years** on the digital services team, saving hard.
Set up a **community advice co-op** with others around 2030.
Keep using **every new tool**, since understanding them is my edge.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a small cold spot about the end of it.
S4.quote: Understanding the tools is my edge until it isn't. Being early is my one real skill.
fieldNote: She'd **ride the wave** for several years, then plan an exit into community work.
With ten years she's willing to **buy a home** and have children around 2030.
She names her own risk: **staying too long** in a comfortable job.

steps.text: Join the ministry's digital services team for three or four years
Set up a community advice co-op around 2030
Buy a home around 2029 while on the higher salary
Campaign for a legal right to retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd be worst off, but because I couldn't help anyone in two years, including myself. What would help is a public income floor that kicks in before the jobs go, and public control of the systems, so the people deciding claims answer to someone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd still want to do this job if nothing changed. I think I would, honestly. The best part of my day is still a human one, the moment someone realises the money is coming.

headlineQuote: The best part of my day is still a human one, the moment someone realises the money is coming.
portrait: Rosa is a 27-year-old **unemployment benefit** caseworker on a pilot team testing an AI triage tool.
She uses **AI every day** and would be mildly disappointed if it all fizzled out.
In the steady picture she expects to **come out ahead**, and feels guilty about colleagues who won't.
In the AGI pictures she plans a move into **community advice work**, accepting a smaller life.
Her progressive outlook shows as calls for **public ownership** and an income floor, not resistance.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she couldn't help anyone, herself included, in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **public income floor** that starts before jobs go.
**Public control** of the systems deciding claims.
